newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street to focus on Microsoft, IBM earnings.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street to focus on Microsoft, IBM earnings.

text.p: High tech heavyweights Microsoft Corp. and International Business Machines Corp. kick off earnings this week with the stock market seen settling into a trading range after the Dow Jones industrial average closed above the 6,000 level for the first time last Monday.

Analysts said that the November elections will again enter the picture on Wall Street with many now worrying that Democrats may take control of one or both of the houses of Congress on President Clinton's coattails.

Microsoft is expected to report fiscal first quarter earnings of 90 cents per share compared with 78 cents a year ago, while IBM is seen reporting third quarter earnings of $2.43 a share compared with $2.30 a year ago.

"The market has been assuming good earnings and, at these lofty levels, if they are in line or disappointing, the two of them could catch cold and move lower," said Alfred Goldman, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.

"If they are better than expected then the market will be pleased for about 20 minutes because right now investors are trying to gauge earnings for the next two quarters and if the market has enough momentum left to go forward," he said.
Even more important than the actual earnings will be what the companies say when they issue their results and the prospects for the industry.

"The real issue is what they say about what the future hold over the next six to eight months," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "The key is not so much whether they meet expectations but what they divulge regarding what the industry is looking at."

Another problem facing high techs in particular is whether they live up to "whisper" earnings, or unofficial forecasts, which exceed the official ones on Wall Street. This is true especially of stocks which have had strong runs in anticipation of the quarterly reports.
Earnings aside, analysts expect the market to enter a trading range or even pull back now that the Dow has topped the 6000 level.

"I expect the primary markets to establish a relatively tight trading range where we will spend a period of time attempting to define the upper and lower boundaries," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
He said he expected a range the Dow to range between 5,900 and 6,100 after closing Friday at 6,094.23, a record high.
Westfalia's Cardillo said that he saw a pullback as the Nov. 5 elections approached.
"Fundamentally nothing has changed but from a technical perspective we are just about overbought and could pull back to to low 5,900s by election time," he said.
While most on Wall Street believes that Clinton will defeat Republican challenger Bob Dole, they are afraid Democrats may regain a considerabele measure of control in Congress.
The Street has been more than satisfied with the executive and legislative branches being controlled by rival parties and are afraid of a breakdown in fiscal discipline.
"Business likes the fact that neither the Congress nor the President have been in a position to do anything of a dramatic nature," said Peggy Farley, chief executive officer at Amas Securities.
"There is the fear that a coalition between the President and the Democratic majority on the liberal side," she said.
